extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of European religious and moral history
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic summary of the social, religious, and political causes that produced hostility and persecution of Christians from the Roman Empire through the early Middle Ages. Identifies popular beliefs, state policies, social disruptions, and theological features that explain antagonism toward the Church.

rubrics_metrics.name: State control of ritual and compulsory national rites
rubrics_metrics.description: The ritual or official religious observances were placed under the control of the Government and made a matter of compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although speculation and philosophical interpretation enjoyed liberty, the Roman state regulated ritual practice and required performance of national sacrifices; this made dissent (or refusal) visible and punishable, and bound public prosperity to conformity with state cults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emperor-worship as a test of loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The Oriental custom of deifying emperors and burning incense before their statues became a kind of test of loyalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice, though not necessarily implying specific doctrinal belief, was viewed as inconsistent with Christianity; conscientious refusal to participate functioned as a political rather than purely religious provocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular belief in divine intervention linking calamities to impiety
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief that our world is governed by isolated acts of Divine intervention and that every great calamity may be regarded as a punishment or a warning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a worldview caused the populace to scapegoat religious minorities for disasters (e.g., 'If the Tiber ascends to the walls... the Christians to the lions!'); earthquakes, famines, pestilence often triggered persecutions on this basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proselytism and desertion of traditional rites
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian missionary activity and the desertion of old temples and rites by converts alienated pagans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike Judaism, Christianity was expansive and converted many Romans; the resulting decline in temple attendance and perceived undermining of traditional worship provoked popular resentment and official concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church as a secret, organised association threatening state security
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church constituted a vast, highly organised, and in many respects secret society which was illegal and likely to excite governmental apprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imperial policy forbade potentially rebellious corporations; a networked, devoted association with opaque meetings and hierarchy could be seen as a nucleus for revolt (Trajan's prohibition on guilds as parallel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of Christians as unpatriotic or inimical to the Empire
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Christians regarded the Roman Empire as a manifestation of Antichrist and some deemed it wrong to fight for their country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This attitude replaced patriotic enthusiasm with a rival loyalty and made Christians appear dangerous to the state’s cohesion and military morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calumnies and moral accusations (orgies, cannibalism, incest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Christians were accused of licentious orgies, eating human flesh, and incestuous intercourse in secret assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secrecy of certain rites (e.g., Eucharistic language, Agapæ) and the withholding of some doctrine from the unbaptised encouraged rumours; such calumnies were persistent, widely believed, and exploited to justify persecution, despite being false according to Christian apologists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy of sacraments and misunderstood rituals as rumor fuel
rubrics_metrics.description: The ecclesiastical rule withheld from the unbaptised knowledge of some mysterious doctrines and veiled a ceremony in obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opaque practices (the sacramental feast, love-feasts, the kiss of love, mystic language about being one body) produced vague rumours that were interpreted as evidence of crimes like cannibalism or incest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-communal animosities (Christian–Jewish tensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual hatred between Jews and Christians contributed to anti-Christian calumny and hostility from both pagans and Jews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christians were reviled by Jews as apostates and traitors (e.g., abandoning national defence), while Jews sometimes fomented calumnies against Christians; the two groups’ friction intensified hostility from the surrounding population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female conversions undermining domestic authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The great number of female conversions caused interference with domestic life and offended Roman notions of household authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman social norms expected wives to follow husbands’ gods; mass female conversion to Christianity and nocturnal meetings were viewed as betrayals of familial duty and provoked intense resentment from husbands and families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular practices (exorcism, superstition) and educated contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices like exorcism were popular with masses but contemptible to educated Pagans; certain superstitions lowered Christians in the eyes of philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While exorcism increased popular appeal, philosophers scorned such practices; the only magical practice seriously persecuted under the Empire was political astrology, not Christian rites, but superstition generally shaped elite attitudes toward the Church.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of exclusive salvation and use of terror imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian teaching that all who dissented must be lost and the emphasis on an eternity of torment for the non‑saved supplied the Church with a powerful, and alarming, instrument of conversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To philosophic minds who prized reason over fear, this use of terror was reprehensible and was even criminalized (Marcus Aurelius' law exiling those who terrified weak minds); it also generated hatred and panic among converts and apostates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intolerance and proselytising rhetoric insulting other cults
rubrics_metrics.description: Christians loudly denounced other religions as dæmon-worship, often insulting worshippers and defacing idols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open invective and active aggression against traditional cults (as opposed to private nonconformity) provoked popular fury and made the Church appear as an intolerant force bent on extinguishing religious plurality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipated suppression of liberty of thought and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the Church claimed to dictate opinions and stigmatised divergent religious views as criminal, freedom of thought and expression came under threat once Christianity gained power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites later events (suppression by Theodosius, murder of Hypatia, closing of Athenian schools) as the consequences of a religious culture that moved from persecuted minority to dominant coercive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church discipline and social ostracism of heretics
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthodox rules forbade ordinary courtesies with the excommunicated or heretics and enforced social separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices such as refusing conversation or common courtesies with heretics, and even exclusion in martyrdom contexts, reflect an institutional intolerance that aggravated social divisions and could justify official or popular hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral excellence and charity as a double-edged cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The Christians’ intense internal charity, moral courage, and transformative effect on individuals gained admiration but did not prevent, and in some ways compounded, external hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their virtues provided striking evidence against calumnies (noble lives and martyrdoms), yet the same distinctiveness and strong internal bonds made them socially conspicuous and contributed to fears of a rival communal loyalty.
